items.followUp: State five differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

rubric.why: Award for correctly contrasting the nuclear organization of the two cell types.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus, whereas eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Name the difference in the presence of a true, membrane-bound nucleus.

rubric.why: Award for correctly contrasting the form of their DNA.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic DNA is generally circular; eukaryotic DNA is linear.
rubric.how: State the typical DNA form in each cell type.

rubric.why: Award for correctly contrasting membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells contain them.
rubric.how: State whether membrane-bound organelles are present in each cell type.

rubric.why: Award for a correct comparison of typical cell size.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells.
rubric.how: Compare the general sizes of the two cell types.

rubric.why: Award for correctly contrasting the usual cell-division methods.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic cells divide by binary fission; eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis or meiosis.
rubric.how: Name the division method for each cell type.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotic DNA is generally circular; eukaryotic DNA is linear.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles.
Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells.
Prokaryotic cells divide by binary fission; eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis or meiosis.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature affects the activity of an enzyme.

rubric.why: Award for explaining the specific fit between an enzyme and its substrate.
rubric.description: The enzyme's active site has a shape complementary to its specific substrate, like a lock and key.
rubric.how: Describe the shape-specific fit between the substrate and active site.

rubric.why: Award for describing binding and formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.description: The substrate fits into the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: State that substrate binding forms the complex.

rubric.why: Award for explaining the result of enzyme catalysis.
rubric.description: The enzyme catalyses a reaction that changes the substrate into product or products.
rubric.how: State that the bound substrate is converted into products.

rubric.why: Award for noting that the enzyme is not used up in the reaction.
rubric.description: The products leave the active site; the enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.
rubric.how: State that products leave and the enzyme can catalyse another reaction.

modelAnswer: The enzyme's active site has a specific shape complementary to its substrate, like a lock and its key.
The substrate fits into the active site and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
The enzyme catalyses a reaction, changing the substrate into product or products.
The products leave the active site; the enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.

items.followUp: Write the word equation for photosynthesis and give one difference between photosynthesis and respiration.

rubric.why: Award for a complete definition identifying the materials, energy source and product of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy and chlorophyll to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
rubric.how: Define photosynthesis and name its essential inputs, energy source and products.

rubric.why: Award for correctly contrasting the main cellular sites.
rubric.description: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts; respiration occurs mainly in mitochondria.
rubric.how: Name the main organelle for each process.

rubric.why: Award for contrasting the materials used and formed in the two processes.
rubric.description: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and forms glucose and oxygen; respiration uses glucose and oxygen and forms carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.how: Contrast the reactants and products of photosynthesis and respiration.

rubric.why: Award for contrasting the energy changes in the processes.
rubric.description: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose, whereas respiration releases energy from food.
rubric.how: State the contrast between energy storage and energy release.

rubric.why: Award for contrasting light requirement or occurrence.
rubric.description: Photosynthesis requires light, whereas respiration occurs continuously in living cells.
rubric.how: State that photosynthesis needs light while respiration occurs continuously.

modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy and chlorophyll to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, whereas respiration occurs mainly in mitochondria.
Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and forms glucose and oxygen; respiration uses glucose and oxygen and forms carbon dioxide and water.
Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose, whereas respiration releases energy from food.
Photosynthesis requires light, whereas respiration occurs continuously in living cells.

rubric.why: Award for identifying parasitology as a biological discipline.
rubric.description: Parasitology is a branch of biology.
rubric.how: Identify the field as a branch of biology.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the subject studied in parasitology.
rubric.description: Parasitology studies parasites and their relationships with their hosts.
rubric.how: State that the field studies parasites.

modelAnswer: Parasitology is a branch of biology that studies parasites and their relationships with their hosts.

items.followUp: Write the steps of the biological method in their usual order.

rubric.why: Award for naming the initial stages of the biological method.
rubric.description: The initial stages are recognition of a biological problem, observation and hypothesis.
rubric.how: Name the problem-recognition, observation and hypothesis stages.

rubric.why: Award for naming the later stages of the biological method.
rubric.description: The later stages are deductions, experimentation, summarization of results and reporting.
rubric.how: Name the stages following the hypothesis.

modelAnswer: Recognition of a biological problem.
Observation.
Hypothesis.
Deductions.
Experimentation.
Summarization of results.
Reporting.

items.followUp: Write two observations that supported the idea that mosquitoes spread malaria.

rubric.why: Award for the observation linking malaria with marshy places where mosquitoes were abundant.
rubric.description: Malaria was commonly observed in places near marshes where mosquitoes were abundant.
rubric.how: State the observed connection between malaria, marshes and mosquitoes.

rubric.why: Award for the observation linking exposure or protection from mosquitoes with malaria.
rubric.description: People sleeping outdoors or without mosquito nets were more likely to contract malaria; nets offered protection.
rubric.how: State an observation comparing malaria risk with exposure to mosquito bites.

modelAnswer: Malaria was commonly observed in places near marshes where mosquitoes were abundant.
People sleeping outdoors or without mosquito nets were more likely to contract malaria.
